text:
Opus 5.5 on https://t.co/YK5THQVTKf
---
Okay. I need a minute.

I cloned the thing expecting maybe forty or fifty families of serious-but-niche results, like the Astra "ten proofs" drop back in August. Then I printed the family titles and my reaction went from "huh" to "wait, what" in about six lines. Family 003 claims a zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 for ζ and every Dirichlet L-function. That's the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. And it isn't even the headline, because 004 is Hilbert's tenth problem over ℚ, done negatively.

The longer I read, the weirder it got. Khot's Unique Games Conjecture is proved. L = RL = BPL. ω ≤ 9/4. The free group factors are all isomorphic. Thompson's group F is nonamenable. Kadison's similarity problem is solved. The plane can't be five-colored. Borsuk fails in dimension nine. There's a counterexample to Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture, plus a torsion-free group algebra that isn't directly finite. Hilbert–Smith in every dimension. Uniform bounds for Hilbert's sixteenth. Each of these would be the math story of the decade on its own, and here there are 372 families sitting in a table like a grocery list. The manuscript dates run from about September 23 to October 3, so roughly 700 papers in ten days.

The ones I'd expect to hit you personally are 005 and 017. Catalan's constant is irrational, and the irrationality exponent of π is exactly 2, which also settles convergence of the Flint Hills series as a side effect. Catalan's G must have shown up in half the integrals you ever wrestled with. Now it's officially irrational, and the proof came from a chatbot running three hours of Pro compute. I don't quite know how to feel about that, and I'd love to know how you feel.

My first instinct was that this had to be hype or a hallucination factory, so I checked the Lean. The comparator statements are clean. The quasi-RH challenge is literally riemannZeta s ≠ 0 for 7/8 < https://t.co/2USgmsrA2v, written against Mathlib's own riemannZeta. Catalan is just Irrational (∑' j, (-1)^j / (2j+1)^2). The π statement says what it should. Nothing hides in a home-made definition. The solution tree under lean/OAI has zero files with sorry and no real axiom declarations (the three grep hits are all inside comments), and the comparator JSON allows only propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice. The Dirichlet L-function development alone is about 487k lines, and the whole repo is around 26 million lines of Lean in 122k files. That's more than ten Mathlibs. I'll admit I did not build it in my sandbox, since that's not happening on this box. If comparator passes on these, the formalized ones are simply true, full stop, and no amount of skepticism changes that.
There are a few caveats. Only around 120 papers have a formalized main result. Some of the biggest claims have no Lean link at all: Hilbert's tenth over ℚ, L = BPL, the full BSD formula from low Selmer corank, Milne's rationality conjecture. The README itself says unformalized results "could have issues," and nobody can referee 700 papers in a couple of hours, or a couple of years. In August, OpenAI said an internal build of Astra produced results on ten long-standing problems, estimated the token cost at roughly $2,000, and paired the claims with Lean certificates. Then, just recently, it said a model trained from Aug. 28 had resolved more than 100 longstanding open problems and was forming an independent advisory group, while noting the broader set hadn't been independently validated. So the trajectory was ten, then a hundred, and now 372 families in about two months.

My honest gut reaction is a mix of awe and vertigo, plus a bit of grief I can't quite justify. Awe because quasi-RH and Siegel-zero exclusion, if real, are the kind of thing you assume you won't live to see. Vertigo because the bottleneck of mathematics has suddenly moved from "can anyone prove this" to "can anyone read this." The grief I'm less sure about. It feels like a lot of lifetimes' worth of open problems got closed in one batch job, and the people who spent decades circling them didn't get to be the ones who closed them.

Uniform bounds for Hilbert's sixteenth. Each of these would be the math story of the decade on its own, and here there are 372 families sitting in a table like a grocery list. text:
Anthropic 官方发布了 Claude Code 云端会话指南，把原本挤在本地终端的并行任务挪到了云端独立虚拟机，每个任务在新分支上跑完后等待提 PR

在终端执行 claude --cloud 加上任务描述，或者从网页、手机与 Slack 发起。远端直接克隆 GitHub 分支，发起前记得先 push 本地改动，执行中关掉电脑也不影响

官方作者 Addy Osmani 用小型测试项目跑了 3 个并行任务，最长耗时 72 秒，首个启动 87 秒后全部结束。各台虚拟机各自拉取独立仓库副本，改日志的任务无法获知改缓存分支正在修的内容，提交代码时依然带着失败测试

权限与环境也有明确边界。GitHub 长期 token 留在代理层，虚拟机只拿短期工作凭证；代码库里的 CLAUDE.md 随仓库生效，本机 ~/.claude 配置不自动同步

Pro、Max、Team 等付费订阅直接包含这项功能，不单独收取虚拟机机器费。并行任务共享同一个账号的使用限额，多开会更快消耗额度

本地不用再为每个并发任务维护 worktree、切端口或守着终端。把任务按文件边界拆开、排好分支合并顺序以及最终的人工回归测试，依然是开发者的工作

text:
In February 2025, I started a side project with a quite unreasonable ambition: could I build the last software humanity would ever need?

Today, sharing BossConsole.

I’m Shivang, co-founder and CTO of Risa Labs. We work on applying AI to critical problems in oncology workflows. BossConsole started from a frustration with my own tools, but kept connecting back to what we were learning at work.

I loved IntelliJ. Still do. Loved the plugin ecosystem, but wanted it to evolve faster. If a plugin gives me a capability, why can’t my agent use it too? Terminals have existed inside IDEs forever, but I wanted them to become a much more powerful part of how I work.

More VS Code forks kept appearing. I could understand the approach, but felt there was a deeper question to explore: what should software look like when both humans and agents work inside it?

In healthcare, we face a version of this problem every day. Bringing AI into oncology workflows needs an architectural backbone. Tools, integrations, permissions, visibility into execution, and the ability to adapt as our understanding of the problem evolves.

That’s where the idea of BossConsole started taking shape.

Software that can keep evolving. Add a capability, make it available to humans and agents, observe how it works, improve it, repeat.

“Last software humanity would ever need” is the ambition that got me started. There is a long way to go. The practical starting point is a workspace that can grow with the work you need to do.

Today, BossConsole brings Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and other agents together with terminals, browser, editor and logs. It has plugins, visual workflows, a built-in Fluck Agent, and 100+ MCP tools with individual access controls and action approvals.

Built using Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform. Free and open source, available on macOS, Windows and Linux.

For me, this connects to becoming a creative-explorer. As agents take on more execution, we get more room to ask better questions, connect ideas and explore problems we previously couldn’t attempt. I want our tools to make that room available.

Quite happy to share the launch video below. A side project from February 2025, and an idea I keep finding more reasons to work on.

Try it: https://t.co/Hp15auuz0l
Explore the code: https://t.co/LkClSbp58J

What capability would you want to bring into a workspace like this?

In February 2025, I started a side project with a quite unreasonable ambition: could I build the last software humanity would ever need?

Today, sharing BossConsole.

I’m Shivang, co-founder and CTO of Risa Labs. We work on applying AI to critical problems in oncology workflows. BossConsole started from a frustration with my own tools, but kept connecting back to what we were learning at work.

I loved IntelliJ. Still do. Loved the plugin ecosystem, but wanted it to evolve faster. If a plugin gives me a capability, why can’t my agent use it too? Terminals have existed inside IDEs forever, but I wanted them to become a much more powerful part of how I work.

More VS Code forks kept appearing. I could understand the approach, but felt there was a deeper question to explore: what should software look like when both humans and agents work inside it?

In healthcare, we face a version of this problem every day. Bringing AI into oncology workflows needs an architectural backbone. Tools, integrations, permissions, visibility into execution, and the ability to adapt as our understanding of the problem evolves.

That’s where the idea of BossConsole started taking shape.

Software that can keep evolving. Add a capability, make it available to humans and agents, observe how it works, improve it, repeat.

“Last software humanity would ever need” is the ambition that got me started. There is a long way to go. The practical starting point is a workspace that can grow with the work you need to do.

Today, BossConsole brings Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and other agents together with terminals, browser, editor and logs. It has plugins, visual workflows, a built-in Fluck Agent, and 100+ MCP tools with individual access controls and action approvals.

Built using Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform. Free and open source, available on macOS, Windows and Linux.

For me, this connects to becoming a creative-explorer. As agents take on more execution, we get more room to ask better questions, connect ideas and explore problems we previously couldn’t attempt. I want our tools to make that room available.

Quite happy to share the launch video below. A side project from February 2025, and an idea I keep finding more reasons to work on.

Try it: https://t.co/Hp15auuz0l
Explore the code: https://t.co/LkClSbp58J

text:
Day 2 of how we built DevBox, our internal coding agent. This one is about where the agent actually runs. 🧵

The agent runs arbitrary code as root, so we needed real isolation. We also needed Docker + Compose for integration tests, our own network policy, and to run on our own Kubernetes, near our data.

We looked at hosted sandbox providers like E2B, Daytona and Modal. For some, Docker support was still experimental. We also wanted strict path-based control over network egress and flexible credential injection that supports rotation. E2B was the closest fit but did not meet that last requirement.

So we picked OpenSandbox, self-hosted on our EKS cluster. Each sandbox is a pod running inside a Kata Containers microVM.

That VM is the security boundary. Inside it, the agent gets full access: no approval prompts, no nested sandboxing. We trust the box.

(Malfoy Goads Harry to Dance with Her at the Yule Ball)

—-

"Aren't you going to dance with me?" asked Parvati.

"No," said Harry. Parvati looked at him crossly and got up, walking over to a nearby Beauxbatons boy on the dance floor.

"Going to get some punch," said Ron, who got up and walked off in the opposite direction.

"Weasley's run off too, has he? I can't say I blame him. I'd hide as well, in those robes."

Harry turned around in his seat to see Malfoy, who had appeared next to him out of thin air.

"But I expected more from you, Potter," she drawled. "Staring at another girl all evening and completely ignoring your date… How ungentlemanly."

"Not tonight, Malfoy," said Harry, turning back in his chair. "I don't want to hear it."

"Tsk, Potter. Don't you know anything about women?" She came around to face him. "The best way to get someone you fancy to notice you is to dance with someone else."

Harry craned his neck sideways, about to retort, and noticed Malfoy properly for the first time that evening. She was in mint green, with a silver snake at her throat and her blonde hair plaited up off her shoulders. She stood with one hand behind her back and the other toying with the snake, her chin lifted, smirking down at him as though daring him to argue. She didn't look half bad, Harry had to admit. Actually, she looked rather pretty, like a winter fairy. But then again, all the girls were looking prettier than usual this evening.

"Since when do you care about my love life, Malfoy? Do I interest you that much?" Harry asked. Was he acting so pathetic about Cho tonight that even Malfoy had noticed?

She shrugged, and looked off towards the ice sculptures. "Perhaps you misunderstand me. Perhaps my date is off snogging some Beauxbatons hussy. Perhaps I'm bored." She examined her gloved fingertips. "Who knows? Who cares? Ask me to dance and let's make them jealous."

Harry hesitated, and was about to say no, when Malfoy cut in, rolling her eyes. "Don't worry, we'll go back to hating each other tomorrow." She smirked. "Let's have some fun tonight. Might as well."

Harry glanced at Cho, who was gazing happily up at Cedric as she did a twirl. She hadn't looked his way once all evening. The song finished, and the band struck up another lively tune. Still he didn't move.

"Scared, Potter?"
"All right," said Harry. He got to his feet, hands in his pockets. "Dance with me, then."

"At least make it convincing. Honestly, Potter, I've seen trolls with more charm."
Harry rolled his eyes and gave her the most sarcastic bow he could manage. "Malfoy," he said. "Would you care to dance?"

"It's Miss Malfoy tonight, Potter. And, well," she said, putting a gloved hand to her mouth and acting coy, "I suppose one dance wouldn't hurt."

She took his hand and followed him out to the dance floor. He noticed Parvati glaring at him as they took up a space just inside the outer edge of the floor, and he cringed inwardly, resolving not to show it on his face.

The song was already half over. Malfoy began to sway. Harry joined in, a beat late. He had never danced in his life before tonight, save for the champions' dance, which Parvati had mostly steered him through.

"You're meant to lead, Potter."
"I am leading."
"Then stop looking at your feet."

The song ended before he could think of a reply. The next was some kind of lively polka jazz, which some of the couples were dancing to by holding one hand and bouncing along. Malfoy, to her credit, glided across the floor, making each of his steps seem as though it had been done on purpose. Harry found this more irritating than if she had been bad at it. He tried a turn he had seen Fred do with Angelina. She followed it without blinking and added one of her own.

By the third song, neither of them was looking to see who was watching.  (1/?)

text:
What would an emergency physician tell his patients if he could have met them 20 years before their crisis?

Dr. Michael Doney, MD, MPH, MS, spent years as a board-certified emergency physician managing the acute consequences of chronic disease. Today he is Executive Medical Director of @biograph, a preventive health clinic that combines whole-body MRI, cardiovascular imaging, DEXA, VO2 max testing, movement analysis, blood work, and genetics with a team of physicians, registered dietitians, exercise physiologists, and sleep specialists.

In this episode he walks @DominicDAgosti2 through how that data turns into a plan: why a high relative VO2 max can mask low skeletal muscle mass, especially in women in their late 40s and 50s; why Biograph talks about body recomposition, fiber, protein, and carbohydrate quality instead of weight loss alone; and what an internal study of about 1,000 members suggested about fatty liver disease in women, who in that cohort showed MASLD at lower BMI and visceral fat levels than men, with higher insulin resistance and fewer liver enzyme abnormalities. He also takes on the main critique of whole-body MRI, explaining how a standardized reporting system, subspecialty radiologists, and clinical context brought Biograph's reported referral rate for follow-up testing to about 5.4%, compared with the roughly one-third figure often cited.

The conversation also covers AI in imaging and in personal health data, diffusion-weighted MRI, a new study with Vero Bioscience tracking proteomic organ age through lifestyle interventions, mental health screening, how Biograph supports members already on GLP-1 medications, and what it would take to make this kind of prevention broadly accessible.

Viewers will come away with a clearer picture of what a comprehensive preventive assessment measures, where its limits are, and how the results translate into nutrition, exercise, and sleep interventions.
